title: Coronary Artery Disease: Risk-Stratify Symptoms and Prevent the Next Event
bottomLine: CAD care separates acute ischemia from stable chronic disease, then integrates symptom burden, functional risk and secondary prevention. Do not let a normal resting ECG or one negative early test close a concerning ischemic presentation, and do not treat stable CAD as only an antianginal problem.
recognize: Exertional pressure, dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance can be ischemic equivalents.
Established CAD automatically raises recurrent-event risk and shifts lipid/vascular prevention intensity.
differentiate: New/rest/crescendo symptoms belong on an ACS pathway; stable reproducible exertional symptoms can follow a chronic-coronary pathway.
Reflux, musculoskeletal pain, PE and aortic syndromes remain important alternative diagnoses.
assessment: Characterize symptom pattern, functional limitation, prior CAD/revascularization, diabetes, kidney disease, smoking, BP, lipids and family history.
Assess bleeding risk and medication adherence/access before intensifying antithrombotic therapy.
workup: Use ECG and appropriate noninvasive anatomic/functional testing based on pretest probability and the clinical question.
Urgent serial ECG/troponin assessment is required when ACS is plausible.
management: Use evidence-based lipid lowering, BP/diabetes/smoking management, antiplatelet therapy when indicated and antianginal treatment for symptoms.
Refer refractory/high-risk symptoms or high-risk testing for cardiology/revascularization assessment.
medicationSafety: Nitrates interact dangerously with recent PDE-5 inhibitors and can worsen hypotension.
Antithrombotic intensity must reflect ischemic benefit versus bleeding risk rather than 'more is better'.
counselling: Teach emergency symptoms and explain that secondary prevention continues even when angina is controlled.
followUp: Track symptoms, function, LDL/BP/diabetes/smoking targets and medication tolerance/access.
examTrap: Treating stable CAD as only a chest-pain problem while ignoring aggressive secondary prevention—or sending home new rest pain because the resting ECG is normal.
oneLinePearl: CAD management has two jobs: control ischemic symptoms and prevent the next vascular event.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society secondary-prevention and ischemic-heart-disease resources

title: Stable Angina: Confirm the Pattern, Then Treat Symptoms and Risk
bottomLine: Stable angina has a reproducible pattern with exertion/stress and no recent acceleration. A change in frequency, severity, duration or occurrence at rest converts the problem to possible ACS; stable management combines antianginal symptom control with atherosclerotic secondary prevention.
recognize: Predictable exertional pressure/discomfort relieved by rest is a classic stable pattern.
Dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance may be an ischemic equivalent.
differentiate: Rest/crescendo/prolonged symptoms are not 'stable' because the patient has known CAD.
Noncardiac chest pain can coexist with CAD; the current symptom still needs characterization.
assessment: Define exertional threshold, frequency, duration, associated dyspnea/syncope, prior revascularization and current antianginal/secondary-prevention therapy.
Review BP/HR and contraindications before adding rate- or pressure-lowering drugs.
workup: Use resting ECG and a guideline-appropriate stress/anatomic test when diagnosis or risk stratification remains uncertain.
Urgent ACS evaluation replaces outpatient testing when the symptom pattern destabilizes.
management: Use beta blocker, calcium-channel blocker, nitrate or other antianginal therapy according to physiology/comorbidity while maintaining evidence-based antiplatelet/lipid/risk-factor care.
Refer refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy/functional testing for cardiology/revascularization consideration.
medicationSafety: Avoid nitrate use with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure and monitor hypotension.
Rate-slowing combinations can produce bradycardia or heart block.
counselling: Teach when a formerly stable pattern has changed enough to require emergency assessment.
followUp: Track symptom threshold, activity, medication adverse effects and secondary-prevention targets.
examTrap: Calling recurrent rest pain stable angina because the patient already has a chronic CAD diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Stable angina is stable only while the pattern stays stable.
sourceBasis: Canadian cardiovascular chronic-coronary and secondary-prevention practice

title: Valvular Heart Disease: The Murmur Matters When the Patient and Echo Agree
bottomLine: A murmur is a clue, not the diagnosis. Symptoms, examination and echocardiographic lesion severity determine urgency; exertional syncope, HF, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction or a new murmur after infection/MI require expedited structural-heart evaluation.
recognize: Aortic stenosis can cause exertional dyspnea, angina or syncope; mitral regurgitation can cause dyspnea, AF and HF.
Many mild murmurs are benign or clinically minor, but a new murmur plus systemic illness can signal endocarditis or mechanical complication.
differentiate: Murmur intensity does not reliably equal lesion severity.
Dynamic flow murmurs from anemia/pregnancy differ from fixed structural lesions but still require context.
assessment: Assess timing/location/radiation, pulses, BP, JVP, HF signs, exertional symptoms, AF, infection and pregnancy.
Ask about prior echo/valve intervention and dental/infection history when relevant.
workup: Use transthoracic echo for suspected significant structural disease; transesophageal/advanced imaging is specialist/question driven.
Compare serial echo only when lesion severity/symptoms justify surveillance.
management: Refer severe or symptomatic valve disease to cardiology/structural-heart pathways and treat HF/AF complications while definitive intervention is planned.
Do not use routine antibiotic prophylaxis for every murmur; prophylaxis is limited to specific high-risk cardiac conditions/procedures.
medicationSafety: Aggressive preload reduction can be hazardous in selected severe fixed outflow lesions.
Anticoagulation in AF depends on valve type/mitral-stenosis context; mechanical valves are not DOAC indications.
counselling: Explain that surveillance/intervention is driven by symptoms and echo severity, not the mere presence of a murmur.
followUp: Use lesion-specific echo surveillance and ensure structural-heart referral is closed-loop.
examTrap: Giving endocarditis prophylaxis for every murmur or reassuring symptomatic severe valve disease because the murmur sounds soft.
oneLinePearl: Murmur + symptoms + echo—not murmur loudness—defines valve risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-valve disease resources

title: Peripheral Artery Disease: Confirm Limb Ischemia and Treat the Whole Vascular Patient
bottomLine: PAD is systemic atherosclerosis with limb consequences. Confirm symptomatic disease with ABI and/or TBI as appropriate, distinguish claudication from neurogenic/musculoskeletal pain, and treat smoking, exercise, lipids, BP, diabetes and antithrombotic risk—not just the leg symptom.
recognize: Exertional calf/thigh/buttock discomfort relieved by rest, diminished pulses and delayed wound healing support PAD.
Diabetes/CKD can make arteries noncompressible and ABI less reliable, making TBI/waveform testing useful.
differentiate: Neurogenic claudication varies with spinal posture and may persist differently from vascular exertional pain.
Acute limb ischemia is a vascular emergency distinct from chronic claudication.
assessment: Assess walking limitation, rest pain, wounds, pulses, skin/temperature, smoking, diabetes, BP, lipids and polyvascular symptoms.
Look for infection/tissue loss and acute six-P ischemia features.
workup: Use ABI and/or TBI to confirm symptomatic PAD and duplex/CTA/MRA when anatomy will change revascularization planning.
Avoid broad routine screening for asymptomatic CAD/carotid disease solely because PAD exists; manage global risk aggressively.
management: Use smoking cessation, structured exercise therapy, statin/lipid therapy, BP/diabetes management and evidence-based antithrombotic strategy.
Refer lifestyle-limiting claudication despite medical/exercise therapy or chronic limb-threatening ischemia for vascular assessment.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic intensification reduces ischemic/limb events in selected PAD patients but increases bleeding; individualize.
Avoid cilostazol where HF contraindicates it and review renal/bleeding risks.
counselling: Explain that PAD is a heart/brain vascular-risk diagnosis too; walking therapy is treatment, not dismissal.
followUp: Track walking function, wounds, smoking, vascular-risk targets and revascularization indications.
examTrap: Treating claudication with pain medicine alone without confirming PAD or addressing systemic atherosclerotic risk.
oneLinePearl: PAD is a limb symptom and a whole-body atherosclerosis warning.

title: Anticoagulation and Reversal: Know the Drug, Last Dose, Organ Function, Bleeding Site, and Urgency
bottomLine: Anticoagulant reversal is not one antidote algorithm. Identify the drug, dose/last dose, renal/hepatic clearance, bleeding severity/site and procedural urgency; stop the anticoagulant, support hemostasis/source control and use agent-specific reversal only when the clinical benefit outweighs thrombosis risk.
recognize: Major bleeding includes critical-site bleeding, hemodynamic compromise, substantial hemoglobin loss/transfusion need or bleeding that cannot be controlled conservatively.
DOAC exposure may persist longer with renal dysfunction and interacting drugs.
differentiate: Warfarin, dabigatran, factor-Xa inhibitors and heparins have different reversal strategies.
Routine PT/aPTT do not quantify all DOAC effects reliably and cannot universally rule out clinically important anticoagulant activity.
assessment: Identify indication, exact anticoagulant, last dose, renal/hepatic function, interacting drugs, bleeding site/severity and thrombosis risk if therapy is reversed/held.
Assess hemodynamics and need for procedural/source-control intervention first.
workup: Use CBC, creatinine, coagulation testing and drug-specific assays when available/clinically useful; do not delay life-saving source control waiting for a perfect lab.
For warfarin, INR is actionable; DOAC interpretation depends on drug/timing/assay.
management: Use local/Thrombosis Canada agent-specific pathways for PCC/vitamin K, idarucizumab, andexanet or protamine where indicated and available.
Restart anticoagulation after major bleeding only after source control and individualized thrombosis/bleeding reassessment.
medicationSafety: Reversal products themselves carry thrombosis risk and should not be used for trivial bleeding.
Renal dysfunction and P-gp/CYP interactions can prolong DOAC exposure.
redFlags: Emergency surgery with active anticoagulant effect
counselling: Teach bleeding precautions and the importance of carrying an accurate anticoagulant list/last-dose information.
followUp: After bleeding, resolve the cause, reassess dose/indication/interactions and document a restart or permanent-stop plan.
examTrap: Giving a reversal agent solely because the patient is anticoagulated despite minor controlled bleeding—or relying on a normal PT to exclude apixaban effect.
oneLinePearl: Reversal begins with five facts: drug, last dose, kidneys, bleeding site, urgency.

title: Aortic Stenosis: Symptoms and Ventricular Consequences Drive Timing
bottomLine: Aortic stenosis severity is an integrated echo/hemodynamic diagnosis. Severe disease becomes dangerous when symptoms, LV dysfunction or other high-risk features appear; exertional dyspnea, angina or syncope in severe AS should trigger prompt valve-team assessment rather than escalating medical therapy indefinitely.
recognize: Classic symptoms are exertional dyspnea, angina and syncope/presyncope; HF can develop later.
A soft murmur does not exclude severe AS when LV output is low.
differentiate: Low-flow/low-gradient states require integrated echo and specialist assessment rather than labeling stenosis mild from one gradient.
Dyspnea in older adults may be multifactorial; symptom attribution still needs careful structural/cardiopulmonary evaluation.
assessment: Assess exertional symptoms, syncope, HF, BP, frailty/function, prior echo progression and goals/fitness for intervention.
Review CAD and conduction disease that may affect valve intervention planning.
workup: Use echocardiographic valve area/velocity/gradient plus LV function and flow context; additional stress/CT testing may clarify selected discordant cases.
Avoid unnecessary frequent echo when mild/stable disease does not meet surveillance criteria.
management: Refer severe symptomatic or high-risk severe AS to a multidisciplinary valve team for TAVR/SAVR evaluation.
Medical therapy treats comorbidity/congestion carefully but does not reverse fixed severe valve obstruction.
medicationSafety: Avoid abrupt excessive preload/afterload reduction in symptomatic severe fixed outflow obstruction.
Do not use nitrates/vasodilators reflexively in hypotensive symptomatic severe AS without acute-care context.
counselling: Teach symptom reporting and activity/driving advice according to lesion severity and current Canadian guidance.
followUp: Use severity-specific echo surveillance and ensure valve-team referral is closed-loop when intervention thresholds are reached.
examTrap: Treating severe symptomatic AS with escalating diuretics/vasodilators while delaying valve-team referral.
oneLinePearl: Severe aortic stenosis is a valve-intervention disease once symptoms or ventricular consequences appear.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-valve disease resources
